response:
READING

**The arithmetic at face value**

Under MORVEDD, Thurlmere becomes 62% of turnover (GBP 1,478,400 of ~GBP 2,401,000) and the total revenue rises by roughly GBP 302,000 over current. Under SALTGRAVE, if Thurlmere leaves entirely on declining the offer, revenue falls to roughly GBP 1,464,000 (Marchgate ~GBP 922,350 + Ostrey GBP 540,200) on 102 tonnes, leaving 62 of the 164 available tonnes empty. The revenue gap between the two paths is real and material: perhaps GBP 900,000 across three years if everything in MORVEDD goes to plan.

The question is whether everything in MORVEDD goes to plan.

**Capacity arithmetic**

Two dedicated jigs yield 82 tonnes of dedicated Thurlmere capacity (2 × 41), yet the contract asks for 96 tonnes. The remaining two jigs must therefore carry some Thurlmere work alongside or the jigs run above their stated average. Either way, with 96 tonnes for Thurlmere and 65 for Marchgate the mill runs at 161 of 164 tonnes — effectively at ceiling, with no buffer for trial work, rejects, or a new customer enquiry. The business would be capacity-constrained as well as customer-concentrated.

**The change-of-control clause is not boilerplate — it has already been fired once**

Vennerdale acquired Thurlmere in 2025. The ink is barely dry. The draft contract gives either party the right to walk on six months' notice following a change of control. Vennerdale have demonstrated they acquire businesses. They could sell Thurlmere, restructure it, fold it into another entity, or be acquired themselves — any of those events could be read as a change of control triggering the exit. This is not a remote tail risk with an established independent mill: it is a foreseeable event with a counterparty that has already made one acquisition move recently.

The practical consequence: the "three-year commitment" is, in realistic terms, a contract that can become a six-month notice to quit. Gallowfield would have spent GBP 96,000, surrendered Ostrey and its 22-year relationship, run the mill to within 3 tonnes of its ceiling — and then been left with Marchgate (unsigned, 65 tonnes) and two jigs wired for a customer who is no longer there.

**The Marchgate problem in each course**

Marchgate at 44% of current turnover has signed nothing. This is a latent threat in both courses but it falls differently.

Under SALTGRAVE: Marchgate is ~63% of the post-Thurlmere contracted revenue base, but the book also carries Ostrey on a signed three-year commitment. The floor is Ostrey's 37 tonnes. Losing Marchgate on top of declining Thurlmere would be severe, but the business still has a contracted customer, a clean balance sheet, and 62 tonnes of spare capacity to market.

Under MORVEDD: Marchgate is about 38% of the enlarged revenue, but the mill is at ceiling so there is no room to diversify in. If Marchgate left, the business would be at 96 tonnes (Thurlmere only) until and unless Thurlmere itself exits. Two customers with one having a soft-exit clause is a precarious structure.

In SALTGRAVE, the correct immediate action is to get Marchgate to a contract. That negotiation is easier if Gallowfield is not simultaneously running at absolute capacity and visibly dependent on Thurlmere.

**Ostrey**

Twenty-two years is not sentiment; it is an operating history that tells you the relationship survives difficult years in the wool trade, survives price cycles, and survives management changes on both sides. Ostrey are now offering a signed three-year commitment at GBP 14.60 — a 41p premium on the current average — expiring 2026-11-28. If Gallowfield releases them for MORVEDD, Ostrey will arrange alternative dyeing. A 22-year relationship rebuilt from scratch is not available on the open market.

**Capital**

GBP 96,000 against GBP 180,000 cash is a 53% drawdown of reserves before the bank facility is touched. The facility is untouched, so the spend is affordable. The issue is not solvency; it is that the GBP 96,000 is non-recoverable if Thurlmere exits. The pumps and the separate liquor circuit have no resale value to speak of, and converting the dedicated jigs back for general use would require further cost. The capex is a one-way door.

**Asymmetry of downside**

MORVEDD worst case: GBP 96,000 spent, Ostrey gone permanently, Thurlmere exits on six months' notice (say, 18 months into the term), mill left with Marchgate's unsigned 65 tonnes and modified jigs. Run-rate revenue collapses to roughly GBP 922,000. The extra revenue earned in 18 months at the MORVEDD premium (approximately GBP 453,000 uplift over current) is partially offset by the capex, and the business is then structurally weaker than before it took the deal.

SALTGRAVE worst case: Thurlmere leaves, revenue falls to ~GBP 1.46m, 62 tonnes need filling. This is painful. The mill has GBP 180,000 cash, an untouched bank facility, a signed Ostrey anchor, and the ability to approach other mills. The business is under-utilised, not existentially threatened.

A 19-person operation whose fixed costs include skilled dye-house labour and the mill building itself can tolerate a period of active business development from a position of no debt and a loyal 22-year customer on contract. It cannot easily survive losing 62% of turnover on six months' notice with no Ostrey fallback and a capex already sunk.

**The revenue shortfall is real but the ceiling on MORVEDD's upside is also real**

Even if Thurlmere runs the full three years without incident, the gain is GBP 907,200 in gross revenue over the term. That sounds significant, but it comes with: near-zero spare capacity, one customer holding 62% of the book under a terminable contract, the 22-year Ostrey relationship destroyed, and no room to diversify. The structural health of the business at the end of the three-year term under MORVEDD — assuming everything goes well — is arguably weaker than under SALTGRAVE, because Gallowfield will have spent three years unable to grow the book while depending on a single large customer that can exit cheaply.

**Recommendation**

SALTGRAVE — with the condition that Ostrey's offer is accepted before 2026-11-28 and that Marchgate is brought to a contract as the immediate priority alongside any effort to fill spare capacity.

---

READING
  Current revenues are GBP 2.1m on 148 tonnes. MORVEDD would add roughly GBP 302,000 per year if it ran clean; SALTGRAVE costs that uplift but avoids the following problems with MORVEDD.

  Capacity: two dedicated jigs yield 82 tonnes but Thurlmere wants 96, so some Thurlmere work must spill onto the other two jigs, pinning the mill at 161 of 164 tonnes with no buffer for new business, errors, or diversification.

  The change-of-control exit clause is not theoretical. Vennerdale acquired Thurlmere in 2025 — one year ago — and is demonstrably an active acquirer. The draft contract's six-month exit on change of control means Gallowfield could spend GBP 96,000, release Ostrey, and be at ceiling — then receive a notice to quit. The "three-year commitment" is, in practice, a six-month notice waiting to be served.

  Under MORVEDD's realistic worst case — exit after 18 months — Gallowfield earns roughly GBP 453,000 in uplifted revenue, spends GBP 96,000 on capex, loses Ostrey permanently, and is left with Marchgate (unsigned) and modified jigs. Run-rate revenue collapses to around GBP 922,000. That is worse than SALTGRAVE's floor.

  Under SALTGRAVE's worst case — Thurlmere walks on declining — revenue falls to roughly GBP 1,464,000 on 102 tonnes, leaving 62 tonnes to fill. The business has GBP 180,000 cash, an untouched bank facility, Ostrey on a signed three-year contract at a slight premium, and the freedom to approach other mills. It is under-utilised, not threatened.

  Marchgate's lack of any contract is a risk in both courses. In SALTGRAVE it can be addressed with time and spare capacity to negotiate from. In MORVEDD the mill is at ceiling and has no room to soften a Marchgate departure.

  Ostrey's 22-year relationship is not a sentimental consideration. It is a proven, stable customer now willing to commit on paper. Releasing them under MORVEDD is irreversible.

  The GBP 96,000 capex is a one-way door: pumps and a separate liquor circuit have no resale value if Thurlmere exits, and reconverting the jigs for general use costs more on top.

  On balance, the asymmetry falls decisively in SALTGRAVE's favour. The upside of MORVEDD is capped by its own change-of-control clause and its capacity ceiling. The downside of MORVEDD is a business left running at less than half capacity with no loyal anchor customer and sunk capex. SALTGRAVE's downside is a revenue shortfall that the balance sheet can absorb while new business is sought. The correct immediate actions under SALTGRAVE are: accept Ostrey's offer before 28 November 2026, open contract negotiations with Marchgate, and begin marketing the spare 62 tonnes.

CALL
  SALTGRAVE

GROUNDS
  The change-of-control exit clause in Thurlmere's contract, held by Vennerdale — an acquirer that bought Thurlmere only in 2025 — turns a nominal three-year commitment into a potential six-month notice, making a 62% customer concentration existentially dangerous for a 19-person business that would have already spent GBP 96,000 and released its sole long-term anchor customer to take the deal.
